label: Fear of failure
title: Bhagavad Gita on Fear of Failure: 7 Verses, Starting at 2.47
description: Seven verses for exams, interviews and launches, starting with Karmanye Vadhikaraste (2.47): the work is yours, the result never was. Sanskrit, plain English and one thing to try.
h1: Bhagavad Gita on fear of failure: 7 verses, starting at 2.47
subtitle: For the exam, the interview, the launch. Read one a day, or all seven before you walk in.
keywords: bhagavad gita on fear of failure
bhagavad gita on success and failure
bhagavad gita verses on fear of failure
gita shlokas for fear of failure
intro: Arjuna's crisis is fear of what his action will lead to. Krishna answers with the most quoted line in the Gita, 2.47: you have a right to the work, never to its fruit. From there the verses show why the result was never yours alone (18.14), why no sincere effort is wasted (2.40), how to stand the same in a win or a loss, and what acting with skill looks like. The last is from the Ramayana, the moment Hanuman is reminded what he can do.

days.heading: The work is yours. The result never was.
days.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
days.forYou: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te: your right is to the action. Fear of failure is a fear about the fruit, which was never given to you to control. Krishna also closes the escape route: don't let this make you stop acting. Care, prepare and aim well, then put the outcome down.
days.today: Write down the result you're afraid of. Under it, write the three actions that are actually yours.
days.note: Plan and care about results as much as you like. Just keep the outcome from owning you.

days.heading: You are one cause out of five
days.line: Every result has five causes: the setting, the doer, the tools, the efforts, and the unseen. You're one of them.
days.forYou: Near the end of the Gita, Krishna lists what shapes any outcome: the setting, the doer, the means, the many efforts, and daiva, the unseen. You are one of five. Fear of failure quietly assumes you're all of them.
days.today: Take one past failure and name the other four causes. Notice how much of it was never yours.
days.note: You still own your part fully. You are one cause among five.

days.heading: No sincere effort is wasted
days.line: No sincere effort here is ever wasted. Even a little of it shields you from great fear.
days.forYou: Krishna says nothing you begin on this path is lost, and even a little of it protects you from great fear. Honest effort stays with you as skill and steadiness, whatever the result.
days.today: Write one thing an old 'failure' taught you that you still use.

days.heading: Win or lose, stand the same
days.line: Hold pleasure and pain, gain and loss, win and defeat as equal. Then step in and act.
days.forYou: Notice the order: first steady yourself about the outcome, then act. Winning and losing will still feel different. You can step forward without your worth riding on which one comes.
days.today: Before your next attempt, say: either way, I'll still be me tomorrow. Then begin.

days.heading: Yoga is skill in action
days.line: Yoga is skill in action: doing the work well, without being bound by it.
days.forYou: Yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam. Once the fear of the result loosens, your attention comes back to the work, and the work gets better. Skill here means doing the task with your whole mind on it.
days.today: Give your hardest task 25 undivided minutes today. No checking how it's going.

days.heading: Do the work in front of you
days.line: Do the work that's yours. Doing something beats doing nothing; even living needs action.
days.forYou: Fear often shows up as not starting. Krishna's answer is plain: action is better than inaction, and even keeping the body alive needs action. Do the next piece, ready or not.
days.today: Do the smallest next step on the thing you've been avoiding, before noon.

days.heading: Hanuman at the back of the crowd

story.title: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
story.body: At the edge of the ocean, the search party looking for Sita stopped. One by one, each warrior said how far he could leap, and none could reach Lanka. Hanuman sat quietly at the back. The old bear-king Jambavan turned to him and reminded him who he was: his birth, his strength, everything he had already done. Why are you holding back? Hanuman stood, grew to his full size, and made ready to leap.
story.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

days.forYou: Fear of failure can make you the quietest person in the room. Let these verses, or a friend, be your Jambavan.
days.today: Send one person a message reminding them of something they're good at. Then ask someone to do the same for you.

verse.sanskrit: बलं बुद्धिश्च तेजश्च सत्त्वं च हरिपुङ्गव । विशिष्टं सर्वभूतेषु किमात्मानं न सज्जसे ॥
verse.line: You have the strength, the brains and the courage. Why are you holding yourself back?

faq.a: Bhagavad Gita 2.47 says you have a right to your actions, never to their fruits; don't make the result your motive, and don't let that turn you towards doing nothing. It separates the effort you control from the outcome you don't.

faq.q: What does the Gita say about failure?
faq.a: That no sincere effort is wasted (2.40), that one who does good never comes to a bad end (6.40), and that every outcome has five causes, of which you are only one (18.14). Krishna asks you to stay the same in success and failure (2.48) and keep acting.

faq.q: Which Gita verse is good before an exam or interview?
faq.a: 2.47 for the fear of the result, 2.38 to steady yourself before you begin, and 2.50 (yoga is skill in action) for the work itself.
